GrowthBook 5.1: Learn faster with a new MCP server, Slack app, and contextual bandits
MCP server, Slack app, and contextual bandits

min read
Helping product teams build, ship, and improve at scale, with AI built into every step.
Every company is trying to do the same thing:
build a better product and move faster than their competitors.
The way to do that is to learn faster, so more decisions are made from evidence instead of guesses.
But learning faster takes more than the ability to run an A/B test.
Your experimentation platform should help you run experiments quickly and rigorously, capture what you learn, and identify opportunities to apply those learnings to the next decision.
GrowthBook 5.1 brings the entire learning loop together, with AI across every step. It’s now available to all cloud and self-hosted users. Check out the full
release notes
for everything that shipped.
Scale testing without sacrificing rigor
GrowthBook 5.1 helps teams scale experimentation, both in volume and in what you can test, like measuring funnel completion or optimizing with contextual bandits. AI-powered workflows remove friction and built-in rigor ensures you can move faster without sacrificing confidence in your results.
‍
Contextual bandits
personalize which variation a user sees at the individual user level, learning which variant performs best based on their context and automatically shifts traffic accordingly. They’re especially useful for time-sensitive campaigns, high-variant tests, or personalization where the best experience varies by user.
Funnel metrics
let you measure funnel completion in your experiments and see where users are dropping off. They are especially useful for testing marketing funnels, onboarding flows, and other multi-step experiences.
AI lets you scale experimentation by turning the workflow into something fully programmable, giving agents the ability to publish flags, create experiments, and more. Our new

The Edge Podcast
How New York Red Bulls Drives Innovation Through Experimentation
Ashley Stirrup
October 29, 2026
Topics
The Edge Podcast
Release
The Edge Podcast
Featured
true
Body
Most businesses evaluate customer value based solely on upfront ticket sales. The New York Red Bulls tested that assumption and discovered that evaluating total matchday engagement offers a far more accurate picture of fan value.
Vamsi Krishna Kunapuli
leads analytics for the club, one of the original MLS teams, founded as the MetroStars in 1996 and rebranded by Red Bull in 2006. The club plays in a 25,000-seat stadium in Harrison, New Jersey, and hosts tens of major events a year beyond its MLS schedule. His team supports the front office across marketing, ticket sales, and partnerships with one core mission: maximizing operational efficiency and driving return on investment.
Vamsi came to sports through a rich background in experimentation. At YouTube Originals, he tested thumbnails and content performance across diverse global audiences. At Fanatics, he tested promotional models and engagement flows at scale. At the Red Bulls, the goal is converting fan touchpoints into stadium visits while ensuring an exceptional fan experience and protecting commercial efficiency.
Rethinking Fan Value Beyond the Ticket
A common assumption in sports business is that high-value upfront ticket buyers always represent the highest total spenders. Through multi-season data analysis and targeted testing, Vamsi’s team learned that fan value is multi-dimensional.
When evaluating attendance patterns and overall matchday spend, including concessions, merchandise, and stadium activations, the data revealed that attendee groups interact with the venue in distinct ways. Single-match attendees, for example, often seek a comprehensive event experience across all stadium touchpoints.
“Even with a lower entry ticket price, a fan's propensity to engage with the full matchday offering can be significant across different areas of the stadium,” Vamsi notes.
Rather than relying on simple averages, the team layers A/B testing onto fan segment comparisons to understand how different promotional structures influence overall engagement and repeat visits. “It's a combination of experimentation and analytics,” he says, “driven by experimentation first.”
Refining the Core Business Metrics
These insights helped evolve how the club evaluates success, moving beyond basic ticket averages to a more holistic view of fan contribution across the entire event visit.
This shift refined marketing strategies, audience segmentation, and outreach models. Vamsi emphasizes that customer segments should never remain static. A definition like “lives within 20 kilometers, attends five games a year” is only useful if continually re-tested. Today, the club refreshes fan segments dynamically, recognizing that every event features a unique opponent, timing, and audience profile.
A Losing Test Isn't a Failure
Drawing on his background in product management, Vamsi views negative test results as essential guardrails.
“A losing test isn't a failure,” he explains. “It prevents you from making costly mistakes.”
For example, if a strategic initiative or pricing adjustment doesn't move the needle, the result still offers valuable data. It clarifies whether price, timing, scheduling, or messaging was the true variable.
His advice for teams is twofold: first, don't let perfection stall execution; second, when an experiment yields negative results, conduct a root-cause analysis. Those learnings fuel smarter follow-up tests.
Host Ashley Stirrup noted a complementary strategy: testing the inverse of a hypothesis to confirm whether a true lever exists. Vamsi agreed: “Sometimes you learn a lot more from an unexpected result than from a successful experiment.”
Aligning Strategy with Clear Organizational Goals
Cross-functional alignment succeeds when leadership establishes clear, shared objectives. Challenges arise when technical and business teams operate in silos without a unified vision.
Vamsi stresses the importance of macro-level thinking: asking how a single change impacts the broader ecosystem and ensuring experiments serve strategic goals rather than existing “just for the sake of testing.”
Data Infrastructure Fuels Creative Ideas
High-quality test ideas stem from asking sharp questions about missing data. Once technical gaps are filled, stakeholders across the organization naturally generate new hypotheses.
Vamsi emphasizes that commercial stakeholders, who live and breathe the operational details daily, should drive the core testing questions. Analytics serves as both a data partner and a strategic thought partner to bring those ideas to life.
Looking ahead, the focus remains on advancing data integration, empowering business units to conduct sound experiments independently, and maintaining a culture of rigor. As Vamsi puts it, hosting every match is like planning a major 25,000-person event. It requires precision, seamless execution, and a clear focus on the outcome.
Key Takeaways
Challenge core assumptions:
Evaluate fan value holistically across all matchday touchpoints rather than relying solely on upfront ticket price.
Align on total value:
Track metrics that reflect overall engagement and operational return.
Embrace negative test results:
Treat failed experiments as valuable data points that prevent missteps and illuminate key business levers.
Keep segmentation dynamic:
Continuously update fan segments to account for event-specific variables.
Empower domain experts:
Let operational stakeholders drive testing hypotheses, supported by robust data infrastructure.
Full conversation with Vamsi Krishna Kunapuli, Director of Analytics at New York Red Bulls, on The Experimentation Edge.

Experiments
Should you cap outliers? Winsorization in A/B testing
Hampus Poppius
October 29, 2026
Topics
Experiments
Release
Experiments
Featured
true
Body
What is winsorization in A/B testing?
Winsorization
replaces every value above a percentile of an A/B test metric, such as the 99th percentile of user revenue, with that percentile. It’s one way to cap outliers. The other is to set the cap at a fixed value. Capping makes revenue metrics much less noisy and experiments faster. This post shows what you gain, what you risk, and when the trade is worth it.
Why everyone tells you to cap outliers
Everybody tells you to cap outliers in long-tailed metrics to gain sensitivity. Your experimentation platform has a setting for it, and every guide to
variance reduction
has it near the top. A key advantage is how simple it is to apply. Set a percentile, and the customers above it get their value replaced by the threshold value before the analysis runs.
If you've felt uneasy about it, you're just like me. The customers above the threshold aren't measurement errors.¹ They're your best customers, and a cap decides in advance that whatever the treatment adds above the threshold doesn't count. The variance argument is compelling, but nobody talks about what it does to your
estimand
, i.e. the quantity you're actually estimating.
This piece is about what made me stop worrying about capping and why I now believe it's what you want to do in most experiments. I simulate experiments with treatment effects that
spread across customers differently
to show what capping does to variance, point estimates, and statistical power in different situations.
The short version is that if you're deciding whether to ship a feature, you want to cap the top 1% or so, unless you expect your biggest buyers to respond much more strongly than the rest. If you need the point estimate itself, for a forecast or a business case, it's a trade-off between the bias the cap adds and the noise it removes.
Who is affected determines the impact of capping
The business setting
Assume an experiment with three hundred thousand customers, where one in ten buys something during the test. Spending among buyers starts around $32, the way a minimum order value works, has a median of $60, and a long tail: the 99th percentile of buyers is at $756, and the top 1% of buyers account for about 13% of all revenue. I also vary the parameters steering this distribution, so the findings can be checked against businesses with more or less concentrated revenue than this one.
In this setup I simulate the same experiment many times over, each time with a new sample of customers, a fresh 50/50 random assignment, and a treatment effect that will take different shapes. I then estimate treatment effects on revenue per customer two ways. Raw, with the values as they are, and
capped
at the 99th percentile of buyers. Note that here, the 99th percentile is among the buyers, i.e. ignoring the 90% of customers who buy nothing. With 10% buyers, this corresponds to the 99.9th percentile of the full sample.
Power
is simply how often each version gets an estimate that's significantly different from zero. The full setup is in the appendix, and the
capping explorer
lets you run the same simulation with numbers that look more like your own.
Figure 1. Spend during the experiment among the ten percent of customers who buy something. The cap is the 99th percentile of buyers, calculated with the zero-spend customers excluded. The 1% of buyers above it account for 13% of all revenue.
Additive vs proportional effects
A treatment doesn't necessarily affect every customer the same way. What a cap costs depends on which customers are affected, so I simulate two different ways that the same 5% revenue effect can be distributed.
Additive effect.
Every buyer spends exactly the same additional amount, $5 in my simulation.
Proportional effect.
Every buyer increases spend by the same percentage, so the biggest customers add the most money in absolute terms.
Both are sized to give the same average treatment effect, i.e. the same increase in average revenue per customer, so the only difference between them is which customers the money comes from. In both, the treatment changes how much buyers spend, not whether they buy.
Real features rarely do exactly either. A common example is a feature that gets some customers to buy who otherwise wouldn't have, while everyone else buys what they would anyway. Those extra purchases are mostly well below the cap, so capping treats that feature almost exactly like the additive effect. The results are almost identical, so think of the additive effect as "similar for those affected" rather than "exactly the same for everyone". The proportional effect stands in for effects that grow with spend.
Now how does capping change your results under these different effect types?
How much precision does capping buy?
Capping does what it promises. In this setting the standard error of the estimate shrinks by about a third, roughly equivalent to doubling your sample size. The reduction is the same for both effect types, because the cap removes the variance coming from the tail, regardless of what the treatment did.
How much you gain in precision depends on how concentrated your revenue (or any metric value) is in the tail, and you can look up where you are (approximately) with one query: what share of your revenue comes from your top 1% of buyers? Our example setting is the middle row below.
Share of revenue from the top 1% of buyers
Standard error falls by
Worth about this much extra traffic
3%
2%
nothing
13%
34%
2 times
29%
73%
14 times
Capping the top 1% of buyers does essentially nothing if your tail holds only a few percent of total revenue. With a long tail holding close to a third of revenue, it's worth fourteen times the sample size, which no other variance reduction technique will get close to. Most businesses selling something online are somewhere in between.
The precision gain is real, but it's also the easy part to show. By reducing the variance of the metric, the variance of the estimator comes down too. Most pieces I've read about capping stop here, or mention a small bias in passing and call it a no-brainer. But what happens to the point estimate?
What happens to the point estimate?
True effect type
Bias of the capped estimate
Additive
0%
Proportional
−13%
Same cap, same data, same
average
treatment effect. One estimate is unbiased and the other is about an eighth too low, and the only thing that differs between the rows is which customers the treatment affected.
Figure 2. Each curve is the distribution of the estimated effect over many simulated repeats of the same experiment, with capping (solid) and without (dashed). The dashed vertical line is the true effect of 5%. The capped curve is narrower in both panels, which is the precision gain. In the right panel the capped curve is centered to the left of the true effect, which illustrates the bias.
Why is this happening? Capping replaces the values of the buyers above the threshold with the threshold itself, in both arms.
Whatever the treatment did to those buyers is erased.
Their contribution to the estimate becomes the same number in treatment and in control, so it's zero.
So the cap removes whatever share of the effect the capped buyers carry. Under a proportional effect, buyers contribute in proportion to what they spend, so that's their share of revenue, 13% here. Under an additive effect they contribute equally, so it's their share of buyers, 1%. The same holds for other spending distributions, as the table further down shows.
That assumes your biggest spenders respond like everyone else (by the same amount or the same percentage). If the effect is more concentrated among them, capping erases most of it, and in the extreme the capped estimate shows nothing at all. They could also respond in the opposite direction, say a price cut that brings in small buyers while your biggest ones pay less for the same basket. In that case, capping removes a negative contribution and the capped estimate overstates the effect.
How much the bias under the proportional effect matters depends on what you use the estimate for. If you're deciding whether to ship, it rarely changes the decision, as the next section shows.
If you need the number itself, it's a
bias-variance trade-off
. The capped estimate is too low on average, but it varies less. When the effect isn't particularly concentrated in the tail, the capped estimate still comes closer to the true effect on average than the raw one does. The raw estimate comes closer only when the bias is large compared to the noise, for example with a feature that mostly affects your biggest buyers.
The bias also carries over to the confidence interval. It's a valid interval for the capped effect, not the uncapped one. As a result, it misses the uncapped effect more often than the stated 95%, and more so the larger the effect.
If you would like to check which customers your effect comes from rather than assume it,
quantile treatment effects
are the natural tool, alongside a
segment analysis
by pre-experiment spend. Compare the 90th percentile of spend between the two arms, then the 99th, and see where the difference appears. This works up to a point. To see the buyers the cap actually affects, you typically need to look further out than the 99th percentile, and that's where the quantile estimate becomes imprecise and the inference harder to get right. It's a useful exercise nonetheless.
A simpler check is to compare the raw and capped results, which GrowthBook shows in the Debug tab of the
metric drilldown
, and to add the same metric capped at a few different thresholds, which is easy with
metric groups
. That shows how much your estimate depends on the customers you cap, but not whether that part is a real effect or chance. We come back to what to make of it when the raw and capped results disagree.
Does capping increase power?
The point estimate might not, however, be the most important outcome of your experiment. If you're just making a shipping decision, what you care about is power. That is, the probability that a real effect is estimated as statistically significant. That depends on the standard error and the point estimate, together. For this purpose, the picture is actually looking quite good, even with the bias.
Figure 3. Power curves. How often an effect estimate is statistically significant, as a function of how large the true effect is. Without a cap (dashed) and with a cap at the 99th percentile of buyers (solid). From the simulation.
At a true effect of 5%, the raw estimate is significant a little more than half the time, i.e. roughly 50% power, whichever of the two effect types it is. Capped, the proportional effect, the one where the cap removes an eighth of the estimate, still has roughly 75% power. Losing an eighth of the effect and detecting it with 75% chance is probably better than keeping all of it and detecting it with only 50% chance. With the additive effect, the best case, capping increases power to almost 90%.
Hence, it comes down to what you want out of your estimate. If you need the number itself, for a forecast or a business case, the cap costs you some bias. Whether the lower variance makes up for that depends on your setting. If you need to decide whether to ship, you need power, and the cap gives you a lot of it for a modest price.
How deep should you cap?
All of that is for a cap on the top 1% of buyers. Whether that threshold is good for you depends on two distributions: the distribution of your treatment effect and the distribution of your outcome metric.
If the treatment effect is large for users at the top of the outcome distribution, capping deeper removes more of the effect. If the outcome distribution has a longer tail, the tail users contribute more noise to the estimate, and capping deeper improves precision more. Capping more deeply helps as long as it removes a larger share of the noise than of the effect.
So think carefully about what your treatment does to the tail users and check the distribution of your metric in the intended audience. If it's hard to make the case that your feature affects big spenders any more than regular users and you have a long tail, you can cap deeper.
In our example, moving the cap from the 99th to the 95th percentile of buyers takes the standard error from about two thirds of the raw one to about half. With an additive effect you keep almost all of the effect, and power rises from almost 90% to almost 100%. With a proportional effect the estimate falls from 87% of the true effect to 70%, and power barely moves, from roughly 75% to 80%.
That's not an argument for capping hard. Whatever the treatment did above the threshold is gone from the estimate, so the deeper the cap, the more of the effect it removes. At the extreme, a cap that reaches every buyer turns revenue per customer into a count of buyers, and an effect on how much people spend disappears from the estimate entirely. If zeros are counted when setting the threshold, that already happens at the 90th percentile of all customers when one in ten of them buys. Cap responsibly.
Does this hold for your data?
Your data might not look exactly like this, so I ran the same comparison across spending distributions where the top 1% of buyers hold anywhere from 3% to 30% of revenue. With a small tail, capping at the 99th percentile of buyers makes no difference. As the tail gets heavier, the power gain grows quickly, and the bias under a proportional effect grows more slowly.

So capping doesn't help when there's little tail variance to remove, as in the top row, where power barely changes. It hurts when the effect is concentrated among the buyers it caps. Otherwise, it increases power.
Your own numbers will differ, and that's what the
capping explorer
is for. Set it up to match your data, and see what a cap does to the estimate and to how often you find the effect. Then try a deeper cap, or a feature that affects your biggest buyers differently, and watch how the picture changes.
When raw and capped results disagree
Most platforms show you both the raw and the capped estimate, and sometimes one is significant and the other is not. When there's no real effect the two rarely disagree at all, less than 5% of the time in this example, and neither direction is more likely than the other. When there's a real effect the disagreement runs almost entirely one way: the capped estimate is significant and the raw one is not. That's what you'd expect, since the capped metric has the smaller standard error and becomes significant first.
So a capped-only result is usually a real effect that the raw metric is too noisy to confirm. The reverse case, raw significant and capped not, is rare. It means the difference between the arms comes from the customers above the threshold, and the two numbers alone can't tell you whether that's a real effect on your biggest customers or a few of them ending up in the same arm by chance.
CUPED
or
post-stratification
make the chance explanation less likely. Nonetheless, treat it as unconfirmed rather than as a win among your biggest customers.
Zeros and per-arm thresholds
"Cap at the 99th percentile" involves two further decisions, and they matter more than the percentile itself.
Whether zeros are counted.
With one customer in ten buying, the 99th percentile of all customers affects the top 10% of buyers. That's probably more aggressive than you intended when selecting the 99th percentile, and it makes a difference. In this setting and with zeros excluded, the proportional-effect estimate drops to 87% of the true effect. With zeros counted, it drops to 59%. You might still gain power, but you're making a bolder assumption about the treatment effect on your best customers.
The fewer of your customers buy, the further down into your buyers the same percentile reaches. So ignore the zeros, and lower the percentile instead if you want to cap harder. Platforms differ on the default, so check
what yours does
.
Whether the threshold is computed on both treatment arms together or on each arm separately.
Most of us have this one backwards. A single threshold for both arms seems fair, and giving each arm its own looks like judging them by different rules. But the single threshold is the more biased one: it gives the biggest buyers in both arms the same value, so the treatment effect on them cancels out. A per-arm threshold moves with the arm, so less of the effect is erased.
What per-arm capping costs is false positives. Two separately estimated thresholds differ by chance, and the usual standard error doesn't account for that, so the false positive rate goes from 5% to around 9%, and higher in heavier tails. Wicker (2026) shows this neatly.²
A standard error that accounts for the estimated thresholds fixes the false positive rate, but at least in this setting, you then get the same power as pooling or less. So per-arm only helps if you care about the point estimate itself, and then it's the same bias-variance trade-off as before: a little less bias for a little more noise.
To cap it off
Capping changes two things at once, and they depend on different things. The variance it removes depends on your spending distribution, the effect it removes depends on your treatment. The trade-off is good when the first is large and the second is small.
Most experiments are run to decide whether to ship something. If that's what you're doing, cap. Unless you expect your biggest buyers to be affected out of proportion to everyone else, the precision is worth more to you than unbiasedness.
Think carefully about how your treatment may affect customers differently. Quantile treatment effects can give you a hunch, but they get imprecise far out in the tail, which is where the cap acts.
If you need the point estimate itself rather than the decision, for a forecast or a business case, keep in mind that the capped estimate is biased by an amount your experiment can't show you. If you don't think the effect comes mostly from your biggest buyers, the capped estimate is still likely the one closer to the truth.
CUPED
and post-stratification reduce variance without adding bias, and they're worth using alongside capping too. Capping needs no pre-experiment data and targets the tail. CUPED and post-stratification work across the whole distribution, as far as your pre-experiment data allows.
Running efficient experiments isn't trivial, and all tricks come with caveats. I'm glad we cleared this one up a bit, so you can more comfortably reduce variance and speed up your experiments. Happy experimenting.
¹ This piece is about capping real values. If you're actually trying to remove erroneous data points, such as bots or test orders, then an
absolute cap
is probably the better tool. You use business context to set it at a value you can defend as implausible for a real customer.
² Till Wicker, "Winsorizing and Trimming in RCTs,"
Journal of Development Economics
182 (June 2026): 103815,
https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jdeveco.2026.103815
.
Appendix: how the simulation works
Each simulated customer has a latent score, drawn from a standard normal distribution. A customer buys during the experiment if the score is above 1.28, the 90th percentile of the standard normal, so that 10% of customers buy. Spend given buying is
spend
= exp(3 + 1.75 ×
score
)
rescaled so that the median buyer spends $60. Because spend is an increasing function of the score and only customers above the threshold buy, spend among buyers has a floor, at about $32, and a long right tail. Because it's a
lognormal
cut off from below, every moment of this distribution is finite. Over the range any single simulated experiment sees, though, its top end behaves like a power law with a tail index of about 2 (the
Hill estimate
over the top 1% of buyers), which is the point at which a true power law's variance becomes infinite.
Two treatment effects are simulated. Additive effect: every buyer's spend is increased by the same amount. Proportional effect: every buyer's spend is multiplied by a constant. For a 5% effect, the proportional effect multiplies spend by 1.05, and the additive effect adds 5% of average spend per buyer, about $5, so both raise revenue per customer by 5%. Two further effect types were simulated during the work and aren't shown: one on the extensive margin, where the buying threshold is lowered so that customers just below it start buying, and one concentrated entirely among the largest spenders.
Each replication draws a fresh population of 300,000 customers, so each experiment is a new sample from the same underlying distribution, not a re-randomization of one fixed population. It assigns every customer to treatment or control independently with probability one half, and applies the treatment to the treated customers. Revenue per customer is then estimated as the difference in means between the arms, with a
Welch standard error
, in two versions: on the raw values, and after replacing every value above the 99th percentile of the non-zero values in the pooled sample with that percentile. A result is called significant if the estimate is more than 1.96 standard errors from zero. Power is the share of replications in which that happens. The false positive rate is the same share when the true effect is zero. The Welch standard error of the capped estimate matches the actual spread of the estimates across replications, so the precision gain isn't a result of understating uncertainty. Power is estimated over 3,000 replications at each effect size, and every effect size is applied to the same 3,000 simulated populations and assignments.
The other results come from additional runs with the same generator and 300,000 customers per experiment, each with 1,000 to 2,000 replications: a sweep of the spending distribution, from one where the top 1% of buyers hold 3% of revenue to one where they hold about a third, covering both effect types and the zeros-included rule; the comparison of caps at the 99th and 95th percentiles of buyers; and the per-arm thresholds. For the per-arm cap, power is computed twice: once with the usual Welch standard error, and once with a corrected one equal to the actual spread of the per-arm estimate across replications with no effect.

TL;DR:
The product and engineering teams we interviewed didn't leave LaunchDarkly to save money on flags that already worked. They switched to get more from one platform. With GrowthBook they were able to:
Turn any flag into an experiment, with results on your own data warehouse and one set of metrics every team trusts
Consolidate flagging, experimentation, and product analytics into one connected workflow (Upstart replaced three tools with one)
Let AI agents create, roll out, monitor, and clean up flags through GrowthBook's MCP and API
Clear years of flag debt and keep it clear with stale flag detection and AI-assisted cleanup
Migrate faster than they expected: the LaunchDarkly Importer moves your flags, and GrowthBook helps with scripts and complex rules
For many teams, the conversation about moving off LaunchDarkly starts with cost, a closer look at the value they're getting, and pressure from leadership to consolidate vendors. But when your flags work today, a lower bill alone may not justify the time and effort of switching platforms.
The strongest case for migration is what GrowthBook makes possible:
feature flagging
,
experimentation
, and
product analytics
together in one platform.
When many teams chose their flagging tool, AI played little to no role in software development and experimentation, and product analytics often lived in separate platforms. Today, AI is accelerating development, expanding what's possible to test, and creating new demands for how teams build and ship products. This turns migration into an opportunity to rethink not only your flagging tool, but the workflows around it.
We interviewed product and engineering leaders at companies that migrated to GrowthBook from LaunchDarkly. This post summarizes why they migrated and the practical lessons they learned along the way, including how AI has changed what teams need from feature flagging.
"GrowthBook gives us the flexibility to self-host and connect our own data sources. Our migration to GrowthBook was straightforward, and its support for both feature flag management and experimentation means fewer tools to maintain and learn."
— Paige Ruppel, Principal Software Engineer, Upstart
Why teams migrate from LaunchDarkly to GrowthBook
GrowthBook’s experimentation capabilities makes the switch worth it
The teams we spoke with told us LaunchDarkly was meeting their flagging needs, even if they didn’t feel they were getting enough value for the price they were paying. Cost savings alone, however, weren’t enough to justify replacing it with a like-for-like solution, as they were comfortable with the platform and switching tools would take valuable engineering time.
In every instance, GrowthBook’s experimentation capabilities tipped the decision and made a clear business case to migrate.
Running both flags and experimentation from GrowthBook
let teams retire homegrown A/B setups, drop separate testing tools, or gave those not yet testing a clear path to start. It also came with the added bonus of bringing
product analytics
into the same platform, leading some teams to consolidate a third-party tool in some cases.
"Experimentation drove our decision to migrate. We probably wouldn't have moved off LaunchDarkly if GrowthBook hadn't offered experimentation on top of feature flagging."
—
GrowthBook user
Consolidation gets you more value and functionality, not just a smaller bill
Feature flagging, experimentation, and product analytics are three steps in the product development loop: ship a change, test whether it works, and see how it moves the metrics that matter. When each step lives in a different tool, the loop breaks. Teams hand off between systems, reconcile metrics that don’t match, and lose the link between what shipped and what changed.
Many teams we interviewed first came to GrowthBook to consolidate vendors and lower their bill. But the biggest value they got was having the whole loop in one place.
Any flag can become an experiment
, every rollout is measured against the same metrics, and the results inform what to build next. That’s value far beyond just a smaller bill.
Here is some of the specific feedback we heard:
Three tools consolidated into one connected workflow.
Upstart was running a third-party flagging tool alongside two in-house experimentation systems. After consolidating all three into GrowthBook, engineers launch experiments in hours instead of days, see results in real time, and quickly catch underperforming experiments. Preloaded, standardized metrics resolved inconsistencies caused by human error, and one tool instead of three cut maintenance and cognitive load. Read the

.
"We had to rally our teams for this project and get our old tools cleaned up, but the process is significantly improving the quality of our systems and reinforcing best practices around experiments and feature-flagging hygiene."

Flag users organically become experimenters.
Any flag can become an experiment, so testing is one step away from shipping. At one company, engineers who were using GrowthBook only for flags naturally started exploring experiments because both lived in the same place.

A clear path to adopting experimentation.
One team we spoke with wasn’t yet running experiments, but plans to as its program matures, which is the reason they selected GrowthBook. They already flag every code change so it can be reverted without a rollback. When it's ready, those same flags will become its first A/B tests.
Measure against one set of metrics.
Another team told us that before migrating, each team had their own metrics and conventions. Their numbers disagreed, and nobody could say which was right. As part of the move, they built a common metrics layer across the organization, so every team now works from the same metrics and tracking, which they fully control. As flags roll out, teams track how those metrics move and use the results to decide what to build next.
"We chose GrowthBook to unify feature flagging and experimentation for better management, along with the depth of control it offers over metrics and data pipelines."
— GrowthBook user
The result is one connected loop for shipping, testing, measuring, and learning what happens after they ship. By tracking how key metrics move as flags roll out, they can see whether changes are having the intended impact and use those insights to inform what comes next.

Lessons learned from teams that made the switch
AI has created new demands for feature flagging
The teams we interviewed selected LaunchDarkly before AI agents became a standard part of software development. As AI transforms workflows, it’s a good reason to reassess whether their existing platform can keep up. AI-driven development creates new demands for how teams release changes, manage risk, and measure impact.
For teams evaluating GrowthBook, support for AI agents was an important consideration. They were either already replacing manual work with agent-driven workflows or wanted the flexibility to adopt them in the future. Either way, they needed a platform that let agents manage the full release lifecycle, from creating and rolling out flags to monitoring impact and cleanup, through APIs and
MCP
integrations directly from their coding environments.
"Long term, we expect more of our day-to-day work to move through AI agents and the MCP server rather than manual UI actions. We eventually want agents to autonomously build and launch experiments end-to-end."
— GrowthBook user
Faster development makes reliable release controls even more important. Teams need to roll out changes gradually, monitor their impact in production, catch issues quickly, and roll back when something goes wrong. Feature flags provide a way to move quickly without exposing every user to a change at once.
These safeguards are also increasingly relevant as teams introduce AI-powered features, where changes to prompts and models may need to be rolled out incrementally and evaluated in production. They let teams ship fast while using
feature flags as a safety net
.
Migration is an opportunity to improve how you ship
The teams we spoke with often set up the basics of feature flagging with LaunchDarkly, established their release workflows, and moved on to other priorities. Over time, flags accumulated, cleanup fell behind, and teams rarely revisited how they managed feature flags or the value they were getting from the platform.
Migration created an opportunity to address that accumulated debt, adopt more advanced release practices, and rethink how teams manage flags over time.
Clean up flag debt to start fresh
Stale flag debt was consistently the biggest hurdle during migration. Teams had to sort through years of accumulated flags, identify which were still in use, retire those that had served their purpose, and decide which to bring over. This process takes time, but it also creates an opportunity for a fresh start rather than carrying unnecessary
technical debt
into a new platform.
Going forward,
GrowthBook's stale flag detection
and AI-assisted cleanup maintains code hygiene by helping teams identify and remove flags that have outlived their purpose.
"Flag hygiene, via the REST API and Claude/Codex tooling through the GrowthBook MCP, is now a regular workflow, not a one-time task."
— GrowthBook user
Move beyond basic feature flagging
Many teams we spoke with were barely scratching the surface of what feature flags can do. Gradual rollouts, ramp schedules, audience targeting, and automatic rollbacks give teams more control over how changes reach users and help manage risk as they release. Migration is an opportunity to rethink workflows, adopt these capabilities, and establish consistent release practices across the organization.
Bring AI into your flagging workflow
Migration is also a chance to identify where AI can make feature flagging more efficient. Many teams are still figuring out where to start, but they don't have to do it alone. GrowthBook partners closely with teams to help them adopt AI-driven workflows and has laid much of the groundwork with a
repository of AI skills

With GrowthBook’s MCP and API, agents can manage feature flags directly from your coding environment, execute release tasks, and automate parts of flag maintenance, all while maintaining appropriate guardrails and human oversight. Templated ramp rollouts can also help standardize how changes are released, giving agents a consistent process to follow.
Migration is faster and easier than teams expect
Migrating feature flagging platforms can sound like a major engineering project. But with a clear plan and support from GrowthBook, your team can control the timeline and make the transition on your terms.
The real time investment is cleaning up flag debt, not moving the flags themselves.
For the move itself,

GrowthBook can also help make the transfer of flags as seamless as possible, including writing migration scripts and guiding teams through the process to handle any complex rules or mapping. You're not left to figure it all out on your own.
For teams migrating both feature flagging and experimentation into GrowthBook, these efforts can run in parallel, minimizing disruption to ongoing work.

The Edge Podcast
A Culture of Experimentation Is a Relationship Problem, Not a Statistics Problem
Ashley Stirrup
October 27, 2026
Topics
The Edge Podcast
Release
The Edge Podcast
Featured
true
Body
Most advice on building a culture of experimentation focuses on evidence. Run more tests, raise your standards, get the statistics right, and the organization will come along.
Shiva Manjunath
does not think that is where programs actually die.
Shiva is a lead strategist at Motive and the host of the
From A to B podcast
, and he has spent much of his career as a solo CRO, the one person in the building responsible for making testing happen. On a recent episode of The Experimentation Edge, almost none of his practical advice was about test design. It was about which teams you talk to before you need anything from them. Below: his bar for what a culture of experimentation actually is, two tests that changed how he reads customer research, and why the fastest way to unblock your
A/B testing
roadmap runs through the sales team.
Shiva Manjunath Sets a Very High Bar for a Culture of Experimentation
He is not grading on a curve. To him, a culture of experimentation means every decision runs through some form of evidence hierarchy, with experimentation as the default rather than the exception. He puts it in the same tier as the greats of any sport: Jordan, Brady, Gretzky. Very few companies live up to it.
"A lot of people might say they have a culture of experimentation, but when it comes to brass tacks, they don’t actually follow that through all the time," he says.
He is careful about what that standard does not mean. Not having the culture is no reason not to test. If you are routing as many decisions as you can through evidence, you are ahead of most teams.
The deeper problem is that the market around the role is still immature. In Shiva’s ideal world, CRO would not exist as a job at all, the same way you would not need peacekeeping bodies in a world that already had peace. Designers, marketers, and product managers would each carry the mindset themselves. The role exists because that mindset is not distributed, and product is where he sees the biggest gap. If product teams genuinely carried it, he says, that would be "the biggest unlock in a company."
Nobody agrees on what the job is either. Ask fifty companies what a CRO does, and you get sixty job descriptions. Product management and engineering are broadly standardized. Conversion rate optimization is not, so most CROs spend part of their first year defining their own role in public.
What Customers Say They Want Is Rarely What They Want
The pricing test that tanked
Shiva’s team ran on-page surveys and asked customers directly what was missing. The answer came back unanimous: show me prices. So they showed prices. Conversion rate tanked.
His read is that the word was pricing and the need was value. Customers can't evaluate the offer, and the closest available word for that is price. When the team rewrote the page around benefits, ROI, and time saved rather than a number, conversion went up.
The research was not wrong. It was literal. Customers reliably name the symptom, and diagnosing what sits underneath it is the researcher’s job. "Always validate through some means," he says.
Edible Arrangements and gifts under $50
When Shiva was at Edible Arrangements, the recurring hesitation was price. People love the product and love the reaction it gets, but "it’s just fruit," and customers were not always willing to pay the higher end prices, especially once delivery fees were added on top.
The response was not a blanket discount. It was a test. They built a dedicated gifts under $50 category for customers who want to send something but don't want to spend a hundred dollars doing it. Clicks into that category and purchases from it were, in his words, astronomical.
It did not stop at the website. The category became printed banners in the stores, and as far as he knows, it is still in use today. A small A/B test turned into a durable merchandising decision, which is also how a program earns its next round of trust. "That was a good idea. What else can we feed in that system?"
Fear, uncertainty, and doubt as a test idea engine
Both tests came from the same habit: asking what fear, uncertainty or doubt sits between the customer and the purchase. Shiva sources it explicitly by asking and implicitly by watching behavior. A spike in traffic to the returns page is a FUD signal even if no customer says the word out loud.
His own example is a custom-fit blind he bought for an awkward window. The anxiety was not price or quality, it was whether a made-to-measure product would fit a window he had measured himself. The company had one thorough install video on YouTube with roughly 100,000 views. He watched it five times before buying.
An install video with a hundred thousand views is a hundred thousand people looking for reassurance before they will spend the money. If you run that site, that is not a support asset. It should be on your highest-signal list of test ideas.
Building a Culture of Experimentation Is a Relationship Problem
This is where the conversation kept landing. The constraint on most programs is not statistical; it is political, and the work of loosening it looks nothing like test design.
The button color trap
If your first conversations with a product team are about green buttons and social proof while they are dealing with real disruption in their business, you lose them before you have run a single test. Shiva’s illustration is a CRO at PlayStation walking into a product org preoccupied with an enormous upcoming game launch, hardware costs and the coming end of disc-based games. Open with a button color test, and the reaction is obvious: "there are so many bigger problems we need to address."
The cost is not just that meeting. Reputations are sticky. "Because you said that button color thing, they’ll keep on thinking of you as just that button color person," he says. He tells every new CRO he mentors to establish authority early, before anyone forms a smaller picture of what you are for.
Build bridges before you need them
The antidote is building relationships before you need anything from them. His metaphor is Chuck E. Cheese tokens. Become the sales team’s best advocate, do the work they ask for, collect tokens, and hold on to them. Then, when a product manager who blocks something that matters, the sales director asking for the same thing moves it.
Sales and support are the two most underused sources of test ideas
Everyone mines analytics. Everyone runs customer interviews. Almost nobody systematically harvests what sales hears on calls and what support hears from frustrated customers.
That is free qualitative data, and it is fresher than anything in your warehouse. Sales knows which objections are trending this month. Support knows which problem generates the most complaints, which is often a fixable experience problem sitting in plain sight.
The trick is to attach a number to it. A support fix is thankless until someone measures it, so treat complaint volume or repeat contacts as a
metric
the test is accountable to. Cut the calls about the same failure by a few percent, and that team becomes your loudest advocate.
Both bridges do double duty: better test ideas, and stakeholders who defend the program when it is under pressure. As Shiva puts it, "your program will take bullets."
Key Takeaways
Take research literally at your peril.
Customers asked for pricing. What they could not articulate was value.
Mine for FUD explicitly and implicitly.
Returns page traffic and a heavily watched install video are research too.
Lead with their problem, not your tactic.
Open on button colors with a team facing bigger threats, and you become the button color person.
Bank favors before you need them.
Sales and support give you better test ideas, and stakeholders who defend the program.
You Do Not Need an Executive Sponsor, You Need a Data-Driven Organization
Not every company will set a CRO up to succeed, and an executive who visibly lives the culture makes everything easier. But Shiva pushes back on treating that as a prerequisite. Without one, it is harder, slower, and more frustrating. It is not impossible. And if the role exists at all, someone senior enough to approve it already believed in the work.
What matters more is whether the organization already makes decisions with data. Experimentation is data. If people do not trust data, they will not trust your results either. So screen for it when you are looking at your next role: listen for whether data comes up unprompted in how people describe their work.
David Massey is a good example of what happens when the foundation is there. When he joined UPS, the company was just starting to explore experimentation, but it was already data-driven. He sold the organization on the potential, and his first test generated $17 million in new revenue. That got everyone’s attention. Today the team has generated over $500 million, and testing new features is simply how the company works.

Protecting your company from the future
Graham McNicoll
October 23, 2026
Topics
Experiments
Release
Experiments
Featured
true
Body
TL;DR: Finding and exploiting bugs is getting cheaper, and the attackers now include software with superhuman abilities. You cannot fix your vendors' security. You can control how many of them hold your data, and where they run. The best security is by removing attack surface areas.
Your customer data can be compromised without anyone breaking into your systems: Every vendor holding a copy gives an attacker another place to look.
This week PHP shipped emergency patches for two bugs,
CVE-2026-109618
and
CVE-2026-109619
, that allow unauthenticated remote code execution on an exposed PHP web server. Both are rated 9.2 out of 10, and CISA told everyone to patch outside their normal cycle.
PHP still runs
almost three-quarters of the websites
, so
there is a good chance something you depend on—a vendor, an agency, a plugin—was exposed for at least a day
. (GrowthBook was not exposed and doesn’t use PHP).
The same day,
a malicious build of LiteLLM
, a popular Python library for calling LLMs, was pushed to PyPI and Docker Hub with a credential stealer inside. It ran at Python startup, before the library was even imported, and went looking for cloud, GitHub, browser, and AI provider keys. The attackers got in through
exposed tokens from three maintainers' GitHub accounts
.
While these are quite different, they point to a growing trend of
AI-driven security exploits and attacks
:
AI has reached a level of understanding code and system interactions that far exceeds even the best security researchers' abilities. The good news is that AI will help patch these vulnerabilities faster. The bad news is that we expect
the number and severity of these attack vectors will keep increasing in frequency and impact
, as AI finds ever more creative attacks.
SaaS Convenience
For twenty years, the standard advice when a company needed tools was to use a SaaS tool, because they're very convenient. But the thing that made SaaS the obvious choice also makes it a target for attackers. Find one exploit, and you get access to hundreds or thousands of company records.
Customer records, usage events, revenue, the behavioral history that runs your experiments and trains your models, are key to your business success.
Now that code is cheap, your data represents a key asset.
It is the one thing a competitor cannot generate with a prompt, and it is the thing every attack above was actually after. The LiteLLM payload did not want the library. It wanted the keys and access to data.
So the question isn’t "build or buy" anymore. It’s “how can I build a robust system that protects my data?”
Exposure is multiplicative
Your exposure is roughly the number of systems holding a copy of your data, multiplied by each system's attack surface.
A typical mid-sized company has copies of its customer data in a CRM, a support desk, a product analytics tool, an A/B testing tool, an email platform, a data warehouse, two or three AI vendors, and a dozen integrations between them. Every one of those vendors represents a surface that an AI attack can target.
How many copies are out there?
One dataset can spread across tools, accounts, and integrations.
Your company
Customer data

Data copy

Data copy
A breach at one recipient can expose the data it holds.
Vendors often don’t reveal how quickly they patch any exploits. Sometimes these patches get stuck behind months-long prioritization schedules.
This is where being open-source is an advantage.
Not only can you easily scan to see if any exploit has been patched yourself, but you can also see how seriously the vendor takes security, and how often they update the product.
You can’t fix a vendor’s security practices.
You can only decide whether they have your data in the first place.
Self-host where you can
The most reliable way to shrink that attack surface area is to
run the systems that hold your most valuable data yourself
, inside your own network, behind your own access controls and firewalls. This is routinely done for warehouses, but less often with platform tools.
Self-hosting does not make you immune to bugs. The PHP vulnerabilities hit self-hosted servers exactly as hard as managed ones. The difference is that with a system that is correctly locked down behind a firewall, there are no ways to run the exploit.
A self-hosted system
behind your VPN
, reachable only by your own services, is not sitting on the public internet waiting for an attacker. A vendor's multi-tenant SaaS tool is.
The second benefit is subtler: Self-hosting is a forcing function for sending less. When it is your database on your disk, you can
give a system only the data it needs
. When you set up a SaaS tool, the integration wizard has to work with all kinds of systems, and it’s often easier to give it permissions for everything rather than just what it needs.
Are there other options?
Yes, and most are worth doing even if you self-host, because self-hosting without them just moves the problem to your own servers.
Warehouse-native tools
are a great way to protect your data. A growing class of tools, including
analytics and experimentation tools like GrowthBook
, run their queries
inside your data warehouse
and never copy the events out. Even if you use our SaaS product, you can still lock down what data it has access to.
Narrow the access
With warehouse-native analysis, raw events stay in your warehouse. You also choose where the tool runs.

Minimize, then minimize again.
Scope every credential
. Rotate on a schedule. Every long-lived, broadly scoped token on an engineer's laptop is a potential vector for attack.
The LiteLLM compromise was three tokens.
Looking forward
The economics of software have flipped.
Building is cheap, and so is attacking. What is scarce—and what is worth protecting—is the data your company has accumulated about its users and its business. You can do a lot to protect these key assets.
At the same time, the rapid development of AI tools is going to cause an ever-increasing number of exploits.
Today, the AI models are the worst they’ll ever be. They are getting better every day.
In this uncertain world, the best advice is to
limit exposure and attack surface areas
as much as possible: Self-host and run the things that hold your data, behind your own firewalls and access control layers, and
give everyone else as little of it as you can.
Get started with more control
Run experiments on your existing warehouse data, with the flexibility to self-host GrowthBook on your own infrastructure.

Experiments
The bottlenecks slowing down your experimentation velocity
Casandra Campbell
October 23, 2026
Topics
Experiments
Release
Experiments
Featured
true
Body
Experimentation
programs can plateau at every scale, whether they’re running 5 tests a month or 5,000. These plateaus are caused by bottlenecks that can occur anywhere in the process, from generating test ideas to analyzing the results.
Most advice about
experimentation velocity
covers how to go faster: prioritize better, automate more, run smaller tests. But if your program is still stuck after applying that advice, the cause is usually one of the
structural, data, or cultural bottlenecks
covered here.
What is experimentation velocity?
Experimentation velocity describes how quickly a program runs experiments: how many tests it completes in a month or quarter, and how long each one takes to get from idea to result.
Each completed test either finds an improvement or rules out a change that didn’t have a meaningful effect, so the more tests a team completes, the more it learns and the more winning changes it ships in a year. Each winning change improves the user experience, and those improvements compound into growth.
Increasing velocity is a central part of
scaling an experimentation program
. It’s important to note that it’s not enough just to run more experiments; companies should be focused on learning more from the experiments they run.
So, while this article focuses on the experimentation process and potential areas of friction, it is equally important to ensure that
new experiments are designed well
with clear objectives and the right collection of primary, secondary, and guardrail metrics.
Why experimentation velocity stalls
A program can only complete experiments as fast as its slowest step allows. The bottlenecks below fall into 3 categories: structural bottlenecks that slow down launching a test, data and infrastructure bottlenecks that slow down analyzing the results, and cultural bottlenecks that keep teams from proposing ideas in the first place.
1. Structural bottlenecks
Structural bottlenecks occur in the process of moving an experiment from idea to launch. They’re the easiest type to diagnose because each delayed test is waiting on a specific step, like a sign-off from legal, an engineer to build the variants, or a QA review.
Endless approval chains
In many organizations, an A/B test requires sign-offs from stakeholders in legal, brand, design, finance, and more, just like a big product launch. Those sign-offs make sense for irreversible decisions with a big blast radius, but controlled experiments are reversible by design. They run on a subset of users for a limited time, and tripwires can stop them as soon as a guardrail metric degrades to an unacceptable level. When every reversible change waits in the same approval queue as permanent changes, tests can spend weeks in review, and teams respond by proposing fewer of them.
You can eliminate most of this delay by right-sizing the approval process. For example, high-risk surfaces like pricing and checkout keep the full sign-off process, while low-risk tests, like onboarding or performance improvements, launch with a single reviewer who checks the experiment against predefined criteria.
Engineering dependency
When every experiment requires an engineer to hardcode variants and deploy them, every test waits on engineering capacity. Each test competes with roadmap work in sprint planning, so it waits for a sprint slot, then for code review, then for the next release. On mobile, an app-store review adds another delay for every hardcoded change.
You can remove the engineering dependency with self-serve test creation. Engineers set up feature flags and configuration parameters once, and product managers use them to build new tests or edit pages directly with a
no-code visual editor
, so a test can launch without a new deployment. AI agents can extend the same self-serve workflow. Connected through an
MCP server
, an agent can create the feature flags and experiments as drafts that a human reviews before they go live.
Downstream QA and deploy congestion
AI-assisted coding and bigger test backlogs produce more variants to validate, but QA and deployment capacity rarely grows at the same rate, an imbalance known as the velocity paradox. Experiments finish development and then wait for a QA review or the next scheduled release, so cycle time doesn’t improve even though the team is producing more variants.
With
feature flags
, experiment code ships dark on the normal release schedule and each test turns on independently, so a finished variant no longer waits for its own deployment or the next release. This approach also allows teams to validate new variants in production. A targeting rule exposes the flagged change to the QA team or internal users first, so each variant gets checked in the real environment without a staging deploy, and a kill switch limits the cost of any bug that QA misses. Because each test runs on its own flag, teams can also
run multiple experiments at once
instead of waiting for one to finish before starting the next.
2. Data and infrastructure bottlenecks
Data bottlenecks usually appear after an experiment launches. Tests start on time, but teams spend weeks validating the results because the numbers live in disconnected tools or because a data scientist has to produce every readout manually. And without a shared experiment repository, teams waste capacity rerunning tests that another team already ran.
Data fragmentation and silos
In many companies, experiment data, product analytics data, and revenue data all live in different tools. Each one uses slightly different tables or metric definitions, like counting conversions per user in one tool and per session in another. An analyst has to explain the discrepancy before anyone trusts the experiment results, and this data reconciliation can sometimes take longer than analyzing the results for insights.
With a single source of truth, no one has to reconcile data across tools. When the experimentation platform reads directly from the data warehouse and every test reuses the same metric definitions, the results in an experiment readout match the figures the business already uses.
Manual statistical calculations
A program that relies on a data scientist for every sample-size calculation, significance test, and data-quality check is limited by data-science capacity. In these programs, a data scientist writes custom queries to pull the results for every test. Health checks that validate the reliability of results, like a test for a
sample ratio mismatch (SRM)
, often run only when someone remembers to request them. Every experiment waits on the same few people.
With an
automated stats engine
, results update on a schedule, variance reduction with
CUPED (Controlled-experiment Using Pre-Experiment Data)
shortens the required duration, and health checks run on every experiment. Data scientists can instead spend their time on difficult experimental designs and on interpreting ambiguous results.
No centralized experiment repository
Without an easily accessible shared record of past experiments, teams repeat each other’s work. A revenue team can test a pricing-page change that the growth team tested 6 months earlier, reach a similar result, and never realize they wasted test capacity on duplicate work. The knowledge from thousands of past experiments, like which ideas failed and which patterns should be explored more, stays with the people who ran them.
A
central repository of past and active experiments
makes that history searchable, so a team can check whether anyone already tested an idea before running it again. GrowthBook’s
Learnings
feature can even start this library for you, using an agent that scans your past experiments.
3. Cultural bottlenecks
Cultural bottlenecks are organizational norms that discourage experimentation. They’re the hardest type of bottleneck to diagnose because they create invisible delays. An executive’s opinion overrides a test result, teams propose only safe changes, or no one sets aside time to generate new test ideas.
The HiPPO effect
In an experimentation program with a HiPPO problem, the highest-paid person’s opinion (the HiPPO) overrides the data. This habit usually predates the program. Product decisions were owned by senior leaders before there was experiment data, and that ownership often stays in place after the program launches. When a director overrules a test result, or a pet feature ships untested, teams learn that running an experiment doesn’t change the decision. They stop proposing hypotheses on anything an executive already has an opinion about.
Organizations can move past the HiPPO effect by making results visible and hard to dispute. When every stakeholder can see an experiment’s design and the analysis behind its readout, they can flag questionable assumptions early, and a leader who wants to override the result has to do it in the open. Each result that passes that scrutiny builds trust in the data.
Fear of failure
Most experiments fail. The median organization sees
roughly 10–20% of experiments
move the metrics they were designed to improve, so a healthy program naturally accumulates losing results. In a team with low psychological safety, where a losing test reflects poorly on the person who ran it, people propose small, safe changes that are unlikely to lose but too small to have a meaningful effect. Velocity can even look fine while teams retreat to safe experiments, because trivial tests still count toward the total. The program produces more experiments and less learning.
Teams that treat an invalidated hypothesis as useful information don’t blame the experimenter when a test loses. A losing test identifies a change that would have degraded the metric if it had shipped. Learning that from an experiment costs much less than learning it in production. When teams evaluate experimenters on the quality of their hypotheses rather than on the direction of their results, people feel safe to propose ambitious changes.
No pipeline of test ideas
Even a team with high psychological safety can run out of hypotheses to test. A program that never schedules time to conduct research and ideate will eventually clear its backlog and resort to filling testing capacity with recycled variations of past experiments.
Teams that
build a culture of experimentation
prioritize hypothesis generation. Regular brainstorms grounded in user research and past results, plus a shared backlog anyone can add to, keep the supply of potential experiments ahead of the program’s capacity to run them.
Removing the experimentation bottlenecks
A program doesn’t need to remove every bottleneck at once. One bottleneck usually constrains velocity more than the others, and improvements elsewhere have little impact until that constraint is removed. If tests launch quickly but analysts spend weeks validating each readout, the constraint is in the data infrastructure, and a faster approval process won’t raise throughput. If analyses come back in a day but the test calendar is thin, the constraint is cultural. Identify the stage where work waits the longest and address that bottleneck first.
The 3 categories of bottlenecks also reinforce each other. Reliable data makes a result harder to override, and a lighter approval process depends on teams proposing enough tests to put through it.
Speed only helps while results stay trustworthy. More experiments produce more
false positives
in absolute terms, so quality checks, like
SRM tests
and
corrections for multiple comparisons
, have to scale with the volume.
How GrowthBook helps remove experimentation bottlenecks
A platform can’t change an organization’s culture, but it can help remove the structural and data bottlenecks. With GrowthBook’s
experimentation platform
, product managers can create experiments from feature flags and configuration parameters, or edit frontend pages with the
Visual Editor
, so most tests launch without engineering involvement.
For example, Lingokids used configuration parameters to
run 2x as many experiments in parallel
, changing paywall layouts and other app behavior through JSON parameters instead of waiting for a new app release. Developers can create feature flags and experiments from their AI coding agents like Claude Code or Cursor, using GrowthBook’s
pre-built agent skills
and
MCP server
to automate steps across the experimentation lifecycle.
Because the platform is
warehouse native
, experiments and
product analytics
read the same warehouse tables with each metric defined once, and readouts match the numbers the business already trusts. The
stats engine
computes Bayesian or frequentist results automatically, supports
CUPED
, and runs an
SRM check
on every experiment, so teams don’t have to wait for a data scientist to run each analysis.
Every past and active experiment lives in one searchable place, and the
Learnings
feature turns their results into a shared knowledge library. The governance gates can be applied only where a program needs them.
For example, feature-flag changes can
require approval
in the environments that need it, while all experiments can carry a
pre-launch checklist
, and
agent-created changes
launch as drafts ready for human review. A
Slack integration
posts experiment launches and results into shared channels, and teams can ask the GrowthBook bot questions about any experiment without leaving Slack. Transparent analyses and shared results make evidence easier to defend.

to see how GrowthBook can remove the bottlenecks slowing down your experimentation program.
Feature Flags
HIPAA compliance: What you need to know for using feature flags
Ashley Stirrup
October 21, 2026
Topics
Feature Flags

Feature Flags

Body
If you build healthcare-related software, you’ve probably been told to make sure that personal health information is kept out of third-party tools. It’s a huge undertaking but necessary considering the consequences of a data leak.
Feature flags
generally make releases safer because you can ship to a small subset of users and turn it off if something goes wrong. But to reach that group, you need
targeting rules
that use patient attributes like diagnosis codes. Those values then flow into SDK payloads and event streams you never meant to share.
In an industry where
the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) logged 663 large breaches
in 2024, you need to account for each path and keep a record of who changed each rule. Even if you sign a BAA with the feature flagging vendor, the safeguards are still yours to build, or at least ensure they exist.
In this article, we’ll explain how HIPAA laws apply to feature flags and how to keep your deployments compliant.
What is HIPAA compliance?
HIPAA compliance
refers to meeting the requirements of the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (1996), which governs the protection of patient health information. For engineering teams, it means following the
HIPAA Security Rule
, which sets safeguards for protecting electronic protected health information (ePHI).
It basically covers individually identifiable health information held or transmitted by a covered entity or business associate. For example, a diagnosis code paired with the patient ID becomes a tracked string of data.
That said, HIPAA doesn’t necessarily apply to every company that works in the
healthcare industry
. It depends on your role in the flow of ePHI:
Role
Who it covers
Where it shows up in your stack
Covered entity
Organizations that deliver or pay for care, like hospitals and health plans
Your organization, whether you’re a payer or a provider. For example, if you offer a health plan or provide care and have access to ePHI.
Business associate
Anyone who creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on a covered entity’s behalf
Your company, if you build software for providers, and any vendor that receives your ePHI
Subcontractor
A business associate’s own vendors that handle PHI
Your vendors’ vendors, like the cloud host behind a SaaS tool
None of the above
A vendor that never receives ePHI or may not be acting as a business associate for that service/data flow
A flag platform that evaluates flags inside your own infrastructure and never receives PHI through its rules, saved groups, metadata, or integrations
The Security Rule groups its requirements into different safeguard categories, and three of them apply to feature flags:
Administrative safeguards (164.308)
cover your policies and people, like access reviews and incident response.
Technical safeguards (164.312)
cover the systems themselves, like access control and audit logs.
Physical safeguards (164.310) deal with facilities and hardware, so they mostly sit with whoever runs your servers. If you’re running a self-hosted deployment, the responsibility is yours. But if you’re using a cloud-based tool, then it lies with the feature flagging vendor and your organization.
You have to implement every spec if it’s a required clause and you have to implement it as written in the safeguard. For example, if the safeguard says that you need a unique user login, then each user needs to have their own login credentials if they can access ePHI. If it’s an addressable spec, you can choose to follow it or document why you chose an alternative because you have the ability to decide if it’s a reasonable requirement for your environment. That’s why security questionnaires these days ask about addressable items like encryption because reviewers want to see the decision you made and the reasoning behind it.
How do feature flags matter for HIPAA compliance?
Feature flags decide which version of your software a user (patient or provider) ultimately sees in the app. And the input to that decision comes down to the attributes it uses, which can include PHI. So even if the feature flagging platform doesn’t store a patient record, it can still end up handling PHI through the attributes you target on, the rules you write, or the integrations around it. Whether that makes your vendor a business associate depends on what actually reaches it.
This matters because data breaches affect your relationship with customers and your market reputation. But beyond that, they’re also very expensive mistakes. IBM’s 2025 report found that healthcare breaches can cost an
average of $7.42 million
. They also take the longest to resolve, with the average breach taking almost 40 weeks to identify and contain. That’s
5 weeks
longer than the global average breach across industries.
Source
In July 2025, Deer Oaks, a behavioral health provider, settled
a $225,000 fine
with OCR after a coding error in its pilot patient portal exposed discharge summaries to the public. In fact, search engines could access and cache those summaries for 18 months. As a result, the company agreed to a 2-year corrective action plan, including audit controls to record and review platform activity.
Unless your feature flagging platform has the right controls in place to catch these types of errors, you won’t be able to limit data exposure.
So, where does PHI really enter a feature flag platform?
First, check where your feature flags are evaluated. For example, in a platform like GrowthBook, the SDK evaluates the flag inside
your
infrastructure, so the attribute values you pass in aren’t sent to GrowthBook. But PHI can still reach it through the rules you wrote or the metadata around it. For example, if you save a list of patients’ IDs as a “Saved Group” for further targeting or experiments, and your team posts the change to Slack, the webhook carries the full diff.
That’s one reason
30% of healthcare breaches
happen through internal actors. You’re operating the way you normally do but unknowingly expose data that was never meant to be public in the first place.

So, your feature flagging platform’s architecture really matters.
Feature flags reduce risk of deployment and help you target users more efficiently, but they come with their own risks:
PHI leaving your app’s infrastructure:
Targeting rules, SDK payloads, event streams, and flag metadata can carry patient data to places it doesn’t need to go.
Unreviewed changes to PHI-handling code:
A flag flip can change production behavior instantly, and it can happen without the review your deploys go through.
You can handle both through a signed BAA and clear approval workflows with timestamped audit logs.
Which HIPAA safeguards apply to feature flags?
OCR has already declared which HIPAA controls generally need improvement. In a
breach report it presented to Congress
in 2024, the following areas were named:
Risk analysis
Risk management
Information system activity review
Audit controls
Person or entity authentication
Each of these maps to your feature flagging layer. It’s common to assume that if your feature flagging tool doesn’t receive PHI, it falls outside the Security Rule, but that’s not the case. The audit controls apply to systems that “contain or use ePHI,” and your flags typically control the code paths that do.
Here’s a list of HIPAA controls that apply to feature flags.
